entries.seminar_title: Physician Networks, Patient Steering, and the Price of Hospital Care
entries.speaker: Jack Cenatempo
Sara Shahanaghi
entries.abstract: An agent decides when to take an irreversible action while learning dynamically whether it will succeed. He is reputation-driven, seeking to signal his ability to learn. In equilibrium, the agent engages in contrarian behavior: he acts for a larger range of beliefs when the prior probability of success is lower. Reputation induces systematic distortions in decision timing: the agent acts prematurely when acting is highly disadvantageous ex ante, and with delay when it is advantageous. Distortions can dynamically reverse under moderate priors, with premature action at the beginning of the research process and excess caution later.

entries.seminar_title: Economic and Environmental Impacts of Broadband: Evidence from the Rural Digital Opportunity Fund
entries.speaker: Junho Choi
entries.abstract: Broadband is increasingly treated as essential infrastructure, comparable to electricity and water, and federal programs are spending tens of billions of dollars to extend it to rural areas in pursuit of economic opportunity. This paper studies the economic and environmental effects of the FCC's Rural Digital Opportunity Fund (RDOF), which allocated $9.2 billion in its 2020 auction. Using a recentered instrument design that exploits variation in buildout timing, extended to exposure through commuting networks, I find that RDOF raises broadband speeds and adoption and increases outbound weekday mobility, but has no detectable effect on telework, employment, wages, or air quality in treated areas. Effects instead arise in commuting-linked areas, where resident employment and residential electricity use decline, manufacturing GDP rises approximately one-for-one with partners' connectedness, NO2 rises, and PM2.5 falls modestly. The results suggest that rural broadband may relocate economic activity and emissions across connected places rather than simply creating or reducing them.

entries.seminar_title: Economic Tradeoffs and Institutional Guidance in Public Resource Allocation: Evidence from U.S. Public Lands
entries.speaker: Maya Norman
entries.abstract: The US federal government owns nearly half of the Western United States, and public agencies, rather than markets, allocate these lands between development and conservation. The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is the primary agency making this tradeoff, deciding where mineral extraction that generates billions in public revenue should proceed and where it should be forgone to conserve one of the least developed contiguous landscapes in the world. Despite the importance of the BLM’s allocation decisions, the mechanisms underlying them have never been studied. Federal law requires the BLM to maximize the land’s market and non-market resource values and publicly justify its choices to stakeholders. But the law does not specify how to value non-market resources or reconcile competing demands from pro-conservation and pro-industry stakeholders. As a result, roughly 150 local offices retain wide discretion over these judgments. Until now, systematically studying how offices exercise that discretion has been infeasible because the evidence is scattered across sprawling planning records and maps. I develop a framework using AI agents to transform these records into a form suitable for discrete-choice econometric methods. I then apply this framework to 11 local offices and roughly 90,000 pages of planning records, recovering how much revenue each office would forgo (i) to conserve non-market resources and (ii) to follow established conservation standards rather than depart from them and bear the burden of justifying that departure to stakeholders. I find that the median office is willing to forgo roughly $60,000 in annual revenue to avoid an acre of disturbance to a non-market resource. I also find that in seven out of ten decisions, the median office passes up the resource-value-maximizing choice to remain closer to an established standard. This tendency to follow standard practice matters for policy. I compare two ways BLM headquarters can steer local offices. One is to recommend a specific conservation practice, such as a one-mile no-drilling buffer around birds’ nests. The other is to use a price-like instrument that specifies the value of conserving a resource. Counterfactuals show that the recommended practice can be as cost-effective as the price-like instrument in achieving the same conservation gains.
